title: Blossoming of Spiritual Path
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk's main teaching is that true growth and development in spiritual communities often arise organically from within, without deliberate planning or imposition of one's own viewpoint. This is illustrated by the example of the Miao Feng Shan pilgrimage site, which grew naturally over time through the contributions of various groups and associations. Reizan Bob Penny suggests that their approach to leading the Wilderness Dharma program this year is centered on participating with nature rather than trying to control it, reflecting a similar organic and natural process in their own community's development.

sentences.text: Good evening.
I apologize if my voice is a little tired.
This is sort of like a dog ate my dharma talk.
Some people know I've been working on trying to save an historic building down in Oregon, but that was always going to be a tough battle and it sort of went down today.
It's not going to happen, so they're going to turn it down.
It's tough fighting big corporations and corrupt governments, and it's really sad to see it happen right in front of your eyes.
We fought the good fight and people are pretty upset about it, but it's time to move on.
I've spent an inordinate amount of time on the phone and typing and everything the last few days and weeks.
So I pulled a book off my shelf for the dharma talk here and I probably spent a couple minutes thinking about it, so here it goes.
A little more might be helpful.
Yeah, thanks.
First, I just want to give people a little update on the Wilderness Dharma program this year and what's going on, because we're right at the beginning of our season, right?
I like to tell people what's going on so that even if you don't get a chance to participate with any of it, you know, and in that sense you can be part of it.
We've added a couple of hikes to the schedule in the early part of the season that we already did, and it feels like we've created an annual schedule here now that has filled out its shape.
One little element that we've added is that our very first hike, our new hike that we went to Lost Lake, starts right down by Larabee, by the seashore, right?

So we got a little glass of salt water and we're bringing that around to all of our hikes, because our cycle of hikes throughout the year travels basically from the ocean up to the glaciers and then back down throughout the season.
In the course of that, we get near the headwaters, the sources of the three branches of our river, the south and the middle and north fork of the Nooksack.
During the course of those journeys, we'll bring this water, and when we do get to those areas, we will exchange it.
At one point we will divide it into three and then exchange it with the fresh water, and then at our closing of the mountains hike, we'll combine it into one and bring it back to the ocean.
Because in our way of doing wilderness dharma here, we've decided to take Dogen's method: if the self advances and confirms the myriad things, that's delusion.
But if myriad things advance and confirm the self, that's enlightenment.
So we don't go out to impose our viewpoint on nature.
We go to just participate with what nature is doing, with the water cycle in this case, to be part of it.
That's a little outline about what all of that is for us here locally, what we're just trying to do, a way of being in our place.
So I want to talk today about this great book, I love this book, *Pilgrims and Sacred Sites in China*, a bunch of scholarly papers about pilgrimage and mountain travel and whatnot.
This is about the pilgrimage to Miao Feng Shan.
Shan is mountain, so Miao Feng Shan is the sacred mountain near Beijing.
It's really a story about the religious development of what's now one of the greatest cities in the world.
Originally, Peking, Beijing, of course they changed the name a little bit.
I don't know if they really changed how they said it or spelled it.
It wasn't so much a Chinese city, because it's very far to the north.
It was more associated with northern tribes, but at some point it shifted, after the Ming dynasty in the 1300s and so on.
The mountain was thought of as Miao Feng Shan, mountain of the marvelous peak, and it lies about 40 kilometers northwest of Peking.
I'll be reading stuff here because that's what I need to do.
*It's the highest of the range of peaks behind the better known Western Hills that rise up inside of the capital.

By comparison with many mountains in China, the history of this peak appears shallow with few layers of cultural significance.* So in that sense, this cult that developed around the mountain had a fertile area to get attached to.
There weren't other deities associated with it as much.
*But the female deity who came to be preeminent in North China by the late 19th century was called P.
Suya.* The cult began by legend, I suppose, in the early 11th century, with a discovery of a female statue lying at the bottom of a mountain pool, but not on that mountain.
*Recovered and installed as an object of worship, this jade woman was able to demonstrate the potency that revealed her as a god.
Although other stories were told about her, most devotees identified this deity as the daughter of the god of the mountain on which the statue was found.* But this was no ordinary mountain.
It was Mount Tai, Taishan, which is the great eastern peak of China.
In China there were many sacred mountains, but of all of them there were five that were the most sacred.
They were the north and the eastern and the southern, the western and the central sacred mountains.
Taishan was perhaps even the most sacred of all, the eastern mountain.
Eventually, over some period of time, some temples were set up that were associated mostly with this cult deity, this feminine deity, and her temples were particularly associated with mountaintops.
Now, the father that she's supposed to be the daughter of was a fearful deity.
But she was being addressed as the heavenly, immortal and holy mother, and by many called simply Nian Nian, our lady.
I think of this as almost like a Virgin of Guadalupe type deity.
Over quite a bit of time, this cult or worship of this deity just grew.
Eventually, a temple was set up on the outskirts of Beijing dedicated to her.
Beijing at that time was a walled city.
There were some temples inside the city, of course, and then there were things outside, out in the countryside.
This was a temple out on the east side of the city.
They called it the Eastern Peak Temple, and they associated it with her because that deity came from the eastern mountain, even though they're up here by the northern mountain.
Then eventually other temples around the city got established and dedicated to her.
One got established on the western side.

By a system, it evolved where the five sacred peaks of China were represented in microcosm in the arrangement of temples around Beijing, and these temples were all associated collectively with this one deity.

It wasn't arranged exactly, completely with the coordinates, but you had the northern summit, and you even had another temple called the Eastern Summit, which was different from the Eastern Peak Temple.
There were many, many temples around the city that developed like this.
It says here, *the temples were very well organized religious associations that drew on both neighborhood and citywide membership.
Annually donated a variety of ritual paraphernalia, pens, ink, paper, record books that were placed in front of the 72 judicial officers as well as flags, banners, incense, and offerings.
Quote, when the god needs something, it's there.
And the concentration of rich, powerful, pious patrons in the capital encouraged the formation and maintenance of these sorts of groups.*
So this was the social construct that started developing around these systems of temples.

At some point, one of these temples, I believe it might have been the Northern Summit Temple, I think it was 700 patrons of that temple who, at some point, there's records, they don't know exactly when it started, right, went to the mountain and established a small shrine.
They put a memorial stone, a stettle, to the deity up there.
It wasn't a very fancy deal that they set up.

*We know that in 1689, the mountain was attracting Peking devotees of Pi Sui, and in the spring of that year, more than 700 men from a temple just outside the city walls who were part of a group were regularly burned incense at the Northern Summit, commissioned a stone stettle to record their visit to Pi Sui Hua Chuan Temple at Miao Feng Shan.* The donors were identified as villagers, and the text was composed and written, because they would put a text on these stones, they'd carve it in, sometimes they'd carve all the people's names, so you learned a lot by reading these stones about what was going on.

*The text was composed and written by a lowly sixth-ranked secretary in the Board of Works, and their stone was small and unprepossessing, a far cry from the huge tablets with elaborately decorated borders, seen in the Temple of the God of the Eastern Peak.*
It was quite remote from the city too.
You had to travel across these barren western hills, and it wasn't a heavily occupied country they were going to.
So that's 1689, right?
But by 1730, it says, *such groups were large and increasingly formalized.
They ranged from a few dozen to more than 700 people, adopted association names and had designated leaders.
The Yinshan Liao Hu [unclear: "Venable"] Association for Leading People to Do Good Deeds, for example, set up their first settle in 1737 with 144 members listed, including a few women.

They erected another 12 years later, naming 163 men, 18 of whom served as association officers, and by 1755, the group had grown to 268, 88 of whom were women, and they identified themselves as people of the banners from the Paofu Temple community outside the northwest gate of Beijing.*
So this type of culture began to evolve of these religious associations, which had lots of different fingers out into the society with secular donors and patrons and everything.

It says here, *in the 19th century, the continuing development of Miao Feng Shan was both mirrored in and made possible by the elaboration of a set of routes to it, for the physical infrastructure and symbolic structure of the pilgrimage grew in tandem.* Eventually there were three main routes to the mountain, the center route, the north route, and the southern route, and they had different qualities.
The southern route became more popular with a lot of people because it was the highway.
It was the easier way to go.
The northern route was used by a group from a city far to the southeast, 40, 50 miles that way, who would travel up and take that route, and I think most people took the center route.

So these different pathways got established, and it says here, *once off the plain, the paths to the summit passed near a few ancient sites, and only an occasional ruined building or crumbling stupa might be seen in the distance.
Miao Feng Shan was a far cry from Mount Wutai or Puto Shan.* These are some of the other great sacred mountains described.
*These names here were of no particular antiquity and merely called attention to natural features in the trials of the ascent.

The 18 turns, the 360 elbow bumpers, melon squashing rocks, fortress ravine, the double dragon ridge, the rest houses and shrines built by pilgrimage associations became the highlights of the trip, and these relatively recent sites directed attention entirely toward the pilgrim's goal.*
*During the climb, one looked up to see if the peak really resembled a lotus flower.

At the summit, one went to peer over the steep temple precipice from which the truly pious could leap without harm, and one sought out the protruding rock behind the main hall that, because of its appearance when struck by sunlight, was given the name Golden Summit.

The stettle erected in 1822 commemorating the construction of a new hall on the peak illustrates the broad scale of activity by that time.* It says many contributors were named, *including incense associations from Beijing and its suburbs, men, women, old, young, Manchu and Chinese, residences and shops, even lime and coal mines from the near hills.*
So all of these businesses and business associations were associated with supporting the pilgrimage efforts.

*With increasing frequency, religious associations were concentrating their activity on specific tasks necessary to the comfort of their fellow pilgrimages.* So the 1822 stone listed 38 rest houses, *literally tea stalls and other altars set up at regular intervals by group.

The stelle also indicated that the goods and services provided already included not only incense, fruit, flowers, altar decorations, prayer mats for the temple interiors at the top and en route, but also tea, medicine, millet, porridge, lanterns, road repair, railings along the river, ropes for the ferry,* et cetera.

What would end up happening by this time, it says here, like in 1852, *we begin to have records of many entertainer groups who were by then and probably had been for some time regular parts of the pilgrimage.
Such groups included, for example, the road openers who frightened off malevolent spirits along the way.
To this end, they painted their faces with fearsome stripes, unloosed their hair and tossed and twisted heavy pitchforks with awesome dexterity.
There were also brightly costumed folk opera troops, drum singers, tightrope walkers, jugglers and a host of other amazing, noisy and colorful performers.
The life expectancy of these associations varied considerably, probably in relation to the degree that membership was reinforced by pre-existing social ties.
Without any significant corporate property, continuity probably depended on the strength of such links and the availability of energetic leadership.*
What they ended up doing is codifying a two-week ritual season at the beginning of April that spanned either side of Buddha's birthday.
For those two weeks, essentially, the city went on pilgrimage.

The way they did it is that in the weeks leading up to that time, the Shoemaker's Association, for instance, or whatever, would be putting up their posters all over town to draw people together into organizing groups to get ready for the effort.
Like the shoemakers, they might have a place that they would set up on the road, a particular rest house might be their province, and they would repair people's shoes.
So they would put up these posters.

Sometimes the posters were cut in the shape of a stella, and they would announce that and have organizational meetings, and it would involve making special clothes and gathering supplies and going out and getting donations for their effort.
Then they would spend the whole two weeks in this.
Most of the time they'd be doing their job, their particular part of the whole pie, fixing shoes, providing tea, whatever it was, being in a juggling troop.
Then at some little window of time, they would say, okay, our time to go to the summit, and they'd go up there for a few days and do their [unclear: "obsessions"] at the summit and then come back.
And this general pattern, it says here, the high tide of this growth of the call to the mountain, *was cut short in late May of 1900.
A great many pilgrims froze to death in a freak snowstorm.* Soon afterwards there was the Boxer Rebellions, and the capital was occupied by foreign troops, and the dynasty came to an end in 1911.
It was only later in the teens, beginning in about 1920, that the cult began reviving and these types of activities really started growing again.

But of course, all that changed in 1949 with the Cultural Revolution, because it was probably just these kinds of activities that the communists couldn't stomach, because with that much devotion going in that direction, it wasn't coming this way to the government, and that wasn't going to work for them.
But what I found in this book is that there are many different such studies of different sorts of pilgrimage roots and associations.
This is just the story of this one: what happens on another mountain and how it grew up and what it became and what it was all about.
Maybe there was a relic that they believed was a piece of the body of Han Shan or something.
It had a completely different flavor, completely different shape, completely different social configuration than what happened here.
Each of these types of things grew organically and then maybe at some other time died organically.
In studying these types of growth of religious movements, I realized, well, why not here?
I see the humble beginnings in which these things begin and how they grow, and it's not something anybody obviously plans.
They just put it out there and keep it going and hope other people join in, maybe or not.
Eventually something happens where people find great association and meaning and it fingers out into society and society sees the importance of that place and their annual connection to it.
That's essentially what we're doing here.
So I think we're reaching the end of our time.
Anyway, somehow I didn't write anything, but I had enough to say.
Thanks a lot.
